utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, perhaps while the witness is being brought in I can just raise one issue. We have not yet received a statement or any submissions in relation to the witness after next who will likely start next week. I just wanted to also point out on the record: Your Honours had issued an order to the Defence to disclose all witness statements. Of course, we have made extensive submissions on the provisions of Rule 67(A)(ii), but even apart from that, Your Honour on the 23rd of June had issued an order for them to disclose witness statements. As we have seen with the last witness -- with this witness the statement was completed on the 1st of June and we received it on the 6th of July. And with the next witness, the statement was completed on the 29th of June and we received it on the 12th of July. So the delay in the disclosures I just wanted to raise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, perhaps you later respond to this, later today, and we would avoid that the witness has to wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bosnic. I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. Jordash will now continue his examination. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bosnic.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could we have on the screen 65 ter 1557.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We were discussing, if you recall, Mr. Bosnic, the re-opening of Golubic, and I just wanted you to quickly look at an exhibit and confirm if it accords with your knowledge of Golubic re-opening.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is consistent with my knowledge of Golubic, at least in part, because I don't know all the individuals concerned or all the activities that took place at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You confirmed yesterday that the Golubic which re-opened in and around September 1992 trained ordinary police officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, just looking at the front page, it notes there that the session was not attended by council member Toso Paic. You see that about seven lines from the top?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You spoke about Toso Paic yesterday; do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How well did you know him in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. He was one of the leaders of the police station in Vojnic. Later on, at my proposal, he became Martic's assistant in charge of Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why did you propose him in the way you testified?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos Pajic told me, and I knew from my conversations with him that he was a highly-trained policeman who had worked with our representation offices in New York and Paris, representing the then socialist Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How often did you see him in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often because we had meetings with representatives of the police who, sometime until mid-1991, refused to accept Martic as a secretary and continued maintaining their contacts with Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is the Vojnic police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, from Vojnic and Vrginmost.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How often would you see him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite often as well. We had meetings to co-ordinate between the civilian authorities, the police, and the army. At the time I was president of the municipality of Slunj and deputy in the Assembly of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did he ever mention to you having any links with the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did he ever communicate any wish or desire of the Serbian DB in terms of the events in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Until mid-1991 he co-operated with Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move to a slightly different subject. I want to ask you about some Babic allegations concerning the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And before I do that, may I tender 1557 as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be D317, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about something Babic spoke about in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: P1878, e-court page 354.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if I can just read the allegation that Babic made and then I'll ask you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I first seek to clarify a matter in relation to the previous document. You asked a question about Toso Paic and then the witness said that he was one the leaders of the police station in Vojnic and later on he became Martic's assistant. And you said "Why did you propose him?" And then he said "Milos Pajic told me, and I knew from my conversations with him that he was a highly-trained ..." So then the qualities of Milos Pajic are set out, at least there could be some confusion. First we were talking about Toso Paic. Now we see during the meeting that Milos Pajic was present. He was also a SUP Vojnic official. So I'm a bit confused by the answer "Milos Pajic told me, and I knew from my conversations with him," and then his qualities are mentioned, which seems to be an explanation for him being appointed in a certain position. Now, was it -- is it Toso or is it Milos?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I think yesterday the witness -- the witness is itching to answer, so, perhaps, I don't know if that's the way to deal with it, if the witness could answer, or I can offer my ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, at least question and answer here are a bit confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, yesterday the witness said that Milos Pajic had recommended Toso Paic to Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the "he" now on page 3, line 8, it is -- we have to read that "Milos Pajic told me, and I knew from my conversations with him that 'Toso Paic' was a highly-trained policeman." That is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- how we have to understand that. I see the witness is nodding, so that's now clear to me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 354 in e-court, and I think we've got that now. Now, Mr. Bosnic, just listen to what Mr. Babic has said and then I will ask you to offer any insight into its truth or otherwise. Babic is asked the following question, line 10: "Q. Now, you were mentioning a moment ago that there were some parallel military units set up by them and led by them, and my question to you is the following: Are you aware, do you know that as far as Serbia is concerned - now I'm being quite specific here, Serbia - as far as Serbia is concerned, paramilitary units were only set up by opposition parties? Do you know that?" Babic's answer: "A. I am aware of the fact that Serbia or, rather, you," that's Milosevic, "via Jovica Stanisic, Radmilo Bogdanovic, and Franko Simatovic nicknamed Frenki, formed volunteer units, detachments, in the SAO Krajina starting with April 1991, and I know that you," that's Milosevic, "instructed and linked up the Secretariat of the Interior or, rather, the police stations on the territory of SAO Krajina, and also that you," Milosevic, "through them, set up special units, the ones that the Assembly of Krajina, on the 29th of May, 1991, called the Krajina Milicija, militia." And then just reading on so you get the full picture. Question from Milosevic: "Q. So the formation of your Krajina police force you considered to be the formation of a paramilitary formation." Answer, page 13507: "A. It was a paramilitary formation because it was not under the control of the government. "Q. How can the police SAO Krajina not be under the control of the government? "A. Well, in the way I explained. It had the right of might and was not subjected to a government that did not have sufficient might. "Q. All right. And what about the Ministry of the Interior? Was he at the head of the police force?" And then line 12: "In such a way that this was done by force, because he didn't wish to hand over his authority which the DB of Serbia and he," that's Martic, "himself had set up, the structure he had set up."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if I may, just to complete the picture, read you another part of Babic's testimony so we know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 1878, e-court page 348, 26 of November, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And again Babic is being cross-examined by Milosevic. And at line 8, Babic, again with reference to this so-called parallel structure, says: "What they were doing," that's Martic and the parallel structure, "was not the structure of the institutions which were legally elected and established at multiparty elections. They were structures which had illegally cropped up, arbitrarily, on their own initiative, and that is why I call them parallel structures to the legal institutions. "And I said that Martic was elected as secretary of SUP. But the Assembly of Krajina, following a proposal by the Prime Minister --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're reading, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "... appointed him Defence Minister for SAO Krajina on the 29th of May. And the very next day, having been convinced by Frenki and people from the DB of Serbia, he," Martic, "refused to hand over to the Ministry of the Interior --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "... and to the newly appointed minister, to hand over his office to Dusan Vjestica. And in that way, it was through the force of might, because, together with the DB of Serbia, he had control over the armed formations of both the police force and paramilitaries which had been set up in the camp of Golubic in April." Did you follow that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The French booth is -- makes an observation that you did not provide them with a copy of this document you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It should be on the screen, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps if there are longer portions to be read it would be good to have them provided in hard copy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So, I want to speak to you, Mr. Bosnic, about Martic and the police and about the allegations that Babic made. Did Martic attend government session meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, that was his obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Babic ever complain to you at the time that Martic didn't attend government meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: For what purpose did Martic attend government meetings? What was his obligation?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As any other member of the government, the obligation was to attend government meetings, take part in discussions in all the items of the agenda, and issue decisions that would subsequently be implemented in the field or forwarded to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And as minister of the interior, was his obligation to report on issues relating to Golubic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would issues relating to the Ministry of Interior or the police force in general be subject to any debate or voting within the Assembly or the government?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. In certain periods of time reports are submitted on the work of each and every minister, and eventually the Assembly is made aware of it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In relation to Golubic, you've mentioned in your statement that a decision was made by the Serbian National Council to set up Golubic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this was misinterpreted to the witness. And if Mr. Jordash would repeat it, then I'm sure the witness will understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 40 of your statement, it states that the decision to set up Golubic in April 1991 was made by the Serbian National Council of which Milan Babic was the president.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Serbian National Council - the B/C/S being "vijece" and not "savjet" - yes, it was headed by Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in paragraph 41 you say: "Milan Martic was not a member of the Main Board of the SDS or a member of the SDS. He was the secretary of the SUP, nominated by Milan Babic, and thus a member of the government?" Do you know how many government sessions were held in and around May and June and July and August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but I suppose that it was frequent, given the situation prevailing in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, you say you suppose it was frequent. Could you try and give some indication, from things you saw or heard, as to whether it was frequent?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do believe that it was frequent. Some -- every seven, eight, or ten days. I know that these individuals came to Knin even more frequently than just to attend Assembly sessions. They had meetings and consultations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you speak to members of the government during the time we're discussing, April to August of 1991, concerning the training at Golubic, the setting up of the Krajina Milicija, and Martic? Did you hear any conversation about that or did you have any personal discussions?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us took part in these discussions, and I mean the political leadership, because we were looking for a way to resist the National Guards Corps and special units of Croatia in view of the fact that we didn't have trained personnel. We were trying to find solutions to the problem. The incursion at Plitvice was the straw that broke the camel's back. That's why it was decided to ask from the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and the Government of Serbia to provide assistance in training young individuals, with a view to setting up a unit that would be capable of successfully resisting the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You say at paragraph 41 of your statement: "If Milan Babic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting. I'd like to intervene in the transcript. The witness did say who took this decision that he is referring to, but that's not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have this verified. You mean the decision which appears at page 10, line 17?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you said that a decision was taken to provide assistance in training young individuals. And who took that decision seeking assistance from the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and the Government of Serbia to provide assistance? Who took that decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian National Council. And it was signed and forwarded to Belgrade by Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know who it was forwarded to?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Government of Serbia and the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know who in the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably to the minister. I suppose that the president of the Serbian National Council addressed the minister, and I think that it was Mr. Bogdanovic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you make mention in your statement that if Milan Babic had not accepted Milan Martic, he would not have gotten the post, the post of the minister of interior. Was it possible -- let me just rephrase that. Was the continuation of a post in the Government of the SAO Krajina subject to votes within the government?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the SAO Krajina, if that is what you mean, was declared the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, the ministers were again elected and so was the government, and as Babic had been proclaimed the president of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, if that is the period that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Had Babic wanted to get rid of Martic in 1991, what would have been the process by which he would have gone about doing that?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he should have either proposed a reconstruction of the government or a new cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not -- let me repeat the question. If Babic had wanted to get rid of Martic in 1991, what would have been a process by which he would have gone about doing that?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would not have proposed his remaining as member of the Government of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina on the 19th of December in 1991. But he was in favour of Martic's remaining, and Martic did remain minister of the interior in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, what's the significance of the 19th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of the Serbian Krajina was proclaimed. Conditionally speaking, the SAO Krajina was abolished and the Republic of the Serbian Krajina was declared in order to keep abreast of Croatia's demands, and Croatia was pursuing independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were those who held government posts at the time of the proclamation subject to re-election?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, and he was re-elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was the process by which he was re-elected?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prime minister designate, who was a representative of the SDS, was given a mandate by Milan Babic to form a government, and at the Main Board there were meetings, there were discussions, about the composition of that government. That was accepted and was as such referred to the Assembly, where it was properly -- where the proper procedure was conducted and they were elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who was the prime minister designate?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Risto Matkovic was the prime minister designate, but essentially it was Babic. It was Babic and we, members of the Main Board, who discussed the members of the government at our session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you present at the Main Board during the discussions about the re-election of Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no discussion at all, in fact. Babic only said or, rather, proposed that Milan Martic should be the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Babic express any misgivings or doubts or in any way appear under pressure about that decision?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in a single moment. This could not be discerned at all and he never said anything of the kind. So it was quite clear that there had been no pressure exerted on either him or anyone else in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now let's return to your statement, D313, and paragraph 56, where you talk about the Knindzes. While that's coming up: Just to wrap up the last issue, why, as far as you could see, did Babic propose unambiguously for Martic to be re-elected? Do you know the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the very beginning of these events, these people from Knin who knew each other prior to the events and from before, so these were people who knew each other from before, and I believe that Milan Babic trusted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you know Dusan Vj estica, the man Babic claimed Martic refused to hand over his office to?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to cast any light on Babic's allegations in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at that Assembly session as I was not an MP at that time, and Babic came up with the idea that a civilian should assume control of the MUP and that Milan Martic should be the minister of defence. However, when this decision reached the people in the field, members of the police actually would not accept Vjestica as minister. They even said that he had had a falling out with the law. I don't know anything about that, mind you. But soon after that the situation was restored to normal and Martic was again the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to give some names of people who were in the field or members of the police who would not accept him as a minister?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the name of the secretaries of the police stations in the various municipalities. That was not within my remit. But as far as I know it was all the secretaries of the police stations in the areas of Lika and Northern Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to the Knindzes. Were you aware of -- well, you clearly were aware of a group known as the Knindzes during 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you give the Court some assistance in relation to the size of the Knindzes, how many people formed the Knindzes?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It was a small group, some 30-odd people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At what point did these 30-odd people become visible to you and other politicians in the region?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they became visible after the first actions which took place in the area of the Krajina in which they participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which action or actions were those?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was the action in Glina, in Skabrnja, I believe in Bruska. That's it, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's it, more or less. Do you know, and I want you to think carefully, apart from Glina and Bruska, are you aware of any other place where the Knindzes participated in combat during 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now I cannot recall whether there had been any other ones. It is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you don't know this but I can tell you this, that in Mladic's diary in 1991 the Knindzes are not mentioned. Is that a surprise to you in terms of military issues and what was going on on the ground militarily, the Knindzes don't warrant a mention in Mladic's diary?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is surprising because all military operations which were taking place in the area were in concert, i.e. -- concert with, i.e., under the command of, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you at the time, you and your colleagues, think of the Knindzes as a significant military force?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the moral [as interpreted] sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That a unit had appeared which was successful, which was taking part in successful operations in co-ordination with units of the Yugoslav People's Army, and that it was a sort of a basis for future sources that would be set up throughout the SAO Krajina, which was later to become the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, P2659.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why do you use the word "moral" in this context, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because our people were afraid. We were afraid that the incursions of the special units of the Croatian police or the National Guards Corps would entail crimes, because we had a negative experience from the period of the Second World War when our people were defenceless.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The word was "morale."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the correction relates to page 16, line 4, the sense of morale, is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is a speech given by Captain Dragan. You've commented on it at page 4 of the chart, D315, and I just want to ask you about some of what Captain Dragan said. If we can -- do you remember this exhibit, Mr. Bosnic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the English page, Captain Dragan says: "I'm not saying that some other units did not take part in this operation." And he's referring to the operation in Glina. "After all, that was a big operation, so-called stinger operation. That was a continuation of wasp operation, where the aim was to clear the MUP forces." Do you have that, Mr. Bosnic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is the third page actually here and you said that in Serbian it was the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon. Do you have the section? It's two-thirds of the way down the page, I think, or perhaps not. It's the section where the heading should say: "Journalist: Would you like to say something about officer Grujica Boric?"

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we go back to page 3. After all, I can see it in the English but not in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It is page 3, you're right, in the B/C/S. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Just read through that to yourself, please, and I'll then ask you --

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: From the point where the journalist asks a question and Captain Dragan says "Just before I move to that issue."

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The journalist: Would you like to say something about officer Grujica Boric?"

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just read it to yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to check whether that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we go over the page, Captain Dragan describes the operation or an operation concerning Glina, and you'll see there where he talks about 21 men from Knin. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if that figure represents the -- at that time the full complement of the Knindzes?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that with certainty. I said that there were some 30 of them. I never counted. And we never asked for the actual number. I suppose that there were only a few of them and they were used more to boost morale than for other purposes, and had they been a larger unit, they would have been much more visible, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you see them in -- moving around?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where and when, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In the areas that Mr. Bosnic was active and in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, on no occasion did I see the mentioned unit in Kordun. Never ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you speak to Babic about the Knindzes at any stage? Did he complain about the Knindzes?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not up to the point when Captain Dragan gave a statement which had to do with politics or the incompetence of the SDS or something along those lines, some statement of Captain Dragan along those lines. Babic interpreted that as Captain Babic's [as interpreted] attempt to interfere in political events in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, on the screen 03879. It's another exhibit relating to Captain Dragan. In the chart it's D298. And it's page 4 of the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you talked about an attempt to interfere in politics in the Krajina, you were referring to Captain Dragan, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When was that, Mr. Witness? When did Captain Dragan give a statement which had to do with politics?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was after these operations in Glina or thereabouts. I cannot be a hundred per cent sure, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When was that? When were the operations in Glina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is a portrait, as we can see, of Captain Dragan. It's dated July of 1991. And the author was an Aleksandra Plavevski. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, just let's go to page 2 of the English and stay with page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's noted, under the title "discipline": "Now, the defenders of the SAO Krajina have highly-mobile assault units ready to act in any part of the territory within only 50 minutes. Special purpose units are positioned in all strategic places in the Krajina, which is now defended in the outer rim areas. They have all the weapons they need, including artillery. Preparations are well underway for the foundation of their own navy and air force." What do you think about that, Mr. Bosnic? Do you have any comment on that journalism?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My comment is the same: This is just nonsense. I have no better word to describe this with. What aircraft are we talking about? Come on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What about "highly-mobile assault units ready to act in any part of the territory within only 50 minutes"?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish. Had we had such units, we would have reached Austria and I would not have ended up in Pancevo as a refugee.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Reading on: "Captain Dragan says that the goal of his units is to lend maximum support to the Yugoslav People's Army, whose legitimacy they recognise fully and which they are ready to defend if required. The function of the special unit is to support the army and the police of the Krajina, and their task is to neutralise the enemy and to eliminate them from the territory of the SAO Krajina if need be."

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This clearly demonstrates that Captain Dragan is confirming what all of us knew and what I have said here, that no military operation could have been carried out without co-ordination with the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did -- sorry, were you going to say something?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And without the knowledge of the Yugoslav People's Army. There was no possibility for independent military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Captain Dragan, as is claimed here, have units, in the plural, or just a unit, as far as you're concerned, as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, Captain Dragan had just this one unit which was called the Knindzes and which had specific patches, the Serbian coat of arms with the four Ss turned upside-down or in the other -- facing the other direction from the regular one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, could we please better explore the basis of the knowledge of the witness. You said you had never seen them. How do you know about their patches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never saw them in action, but these men who completed their training and returned to the area of Kordun wore the uniforms of the Krajina Milicija. And I saw Captain Dragan in Knin and I also saw a man by the nickname of Cigo and I saw the commander of the armoured train, his name was Blagoje Guska, and they wore these uniforms and they had red berets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let me try to understand your testimony. You said you saw these men who had completed their training and returned to the area of Kordun wearing these uniforms. Now, in your written statement you are talking about part of the first group that was trained in Golubic stayed there to train others, and you said that was the group known as the Knindzes, and they became a special unit of the police. Then you described where they came from, that they participated in combat on the territory of Dalmatia and Lika if necessary, and that they participated in an operation in Glina, and you said they were never in Kordun. Apparently describing the patches, you are talking about people that were trained, not part of the first group but apparently a follow-up group, who went back to Kordun. You described their patches, although you say Knindzes, that was the first group that in part stayed for purposes of training others, I take it that these are your volunteers, and they later participated in combat actions and they never came to Kordun. When I ask you how you knew about the patches of the Knindzes, you tell me that you saw them at the uniforms of people who came back to Kordun, but that is not the group which in your written statement is described as the Knindzes. So I'm totally confused by what you are telling us. Mr. Jordash, if you could create any clarity in this respect. And the reason why I ask for the basis of the knowledge is that of course the witness says, I assume that there were little - without or what that assumption was based is rather unclear at numbers. He never counted them, he never got reports about the numbers, so he assumes that they were smaller numbers. Why he does assume so is -- again, is also totally unclear to me. So it's -- this is just an example of what I find confusing at this moment. And if you could clarify it, that certainly would assist me and hopefully my colleagues as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You followed the President's query, Mr. Bosnic? Let's try to break it down.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you include within the Knindzes those who were trained at Golubic who then returned to, for example, Kordun?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were members of Martic's Police. That's how they were called. Only those who stayed back in Knin under Captain Dragan's command, in other words, the best men of those who had trained, were under his command. And that's why they had, being the Knindzes, different sort of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And those who did not stay in Knin under Captain Dragan's command, where did they operate from?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They operated from the municipalities whence they had originally come, and they were under the command of the MUP of the Krajina, in other words, Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had blue camouflage uniforms with a large sign saying Milicija Krajina, Krajina's Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you see that? Did you see the uniform? Did you see Krajina's Police wearing that uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Ilija Saula, Medakovic, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, putting that group of people aside and returning to the men in Knin under Captain Dragan's command, where were they based in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were stationed in Golubic, and Captain Dragan was in the Knin fortress.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you actually see that group in Golubic or outside of Golubic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The individuals that I named I saw in town. As for those others, I heard about them at the meetings where we discussed these issues. But the three individuals I mentioned before were ones that I saw in town, and that's why I can tell you what their uniforms were like. But I didn't see them in action.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which three individuals did you see?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Dragan; Blagoje Guska, who was the commander of the armoured train which was part of the Knindze unit; and a local, a man they referred to as Cigo, I forgot his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you saw those three and then you said that you also discussed the others at meetings. Which meetings were these men the subject of discussion?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it was said that the training at Golubic was successful in churning up a small number of individuals from the general area who would make up this special unit, whereas others were to remain -- to go back to the areas they had originally come from for that specific training in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, would you mind to go back now to the original question where it all started. What patches then did these Knindzes have? Not the ones who returned to their own locations, but where you said you saw three of them in town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had camouflage uniforms but they were military uniforms, green.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wasn't asking about uniforms. I was asking about patches on the uniforms. Could you describe those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian coat of arms but one where the Ss are facing away from each other, whereas normally they would be facing one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they wear red berets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On what is your knowledge based that there was only one unit and not several units of these Knindzes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at the meetings we discussed only this one unit. I didn't have any information to the effect that there were any in Banija and I knew that there weren't any in Kordun. Had there been any other units of the sort, we would have known it. We were politically active and had contacts at these meetings with representatives of the police and the army. There was never any mention of units other than this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you have no positive knowledge, it's just what you discussed and that you never discussed more than one unit, you never saw more than one unit, so therefore you assume that it was one single unit; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am certain to a great extent because I travelled the area and I had never heard of another unit existing. But in substance, my answer to what you just said is yes. The travels I made in the area would have put me on notice of the existence of another such unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's at least clear from where your level of certainty derives. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who were you talking to at that point in time who you might have expected to hear about the existence of more than one unit? Please give a selection of people who you might have expected to hear that from but didn't.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the area of Kordun, I would certainly have heard it from Milos or Toso Paic, from the commanders of TO staffs, or representatives of the JNA at the meetings I attended. At times there were discussions about actions that had been conducted, but there had never been any mention of another special unit, hence my opinion that there could not have been another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your opinion was that there was not another one. I'm just trying to understand. If not -- if there was no conversation about a second unit, to conclude that there could not be one is quite a different opinion from that there was not another one. And, Mr. Jordash, I'm really concerned about mixing up opinions, assumptions, facts known to the witness. Could you please try, in what now follows, to always clearly distinguish between knowledge of facts, personal observation, or hearsay so that it's always clear what we are hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say "I never heard talking about it, so there could not have been another one," that's a kind of an opinion which really doesn't assist the Chamber. But if you say I have no reasons to believe that there was another one, that's fine. That's a conclusion you can draw. But to say that it was never discussed so that on that is based my opinion that there could not be another one is of course something totally different. I take it that you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The one excludes a possibility and the other one leaves it open that there may have been or there may not have been but -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I think there's overlap between the two depending upon where the witness received his -- what conversations the witness had. There comes a point when the number of conversations the witness has had about a unit reaches the point where the witness can be certain there wasn't more than one unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a kind of a conclusion which is not -- unless -- you need a lot of factual bases before you can come to such a conclusion, and not just a few conversations here and there in a relatively large area where a unit apparently is 30 people, 30 to 40. But let's not end up in a discussion. I tried to explain what was on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the witness has described the basis for his opinion, as Your Honour sees it, and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should try to clarify it since it's still on the basis of opinion. Let's break it down, Mr. Bosnic. You spoke to Toso Paic; why would you have expected him to mention if there was more than one unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, representatives of the civilian government and the SDS would have been informed of a unit appearing in the area of Kordun coming from elsewhere. We attended meetings of the zone TO staff where no other unit had been mentioned. After the operation Slunj, Mr. Cedo Bulat only referred to TO and JNA units. The TO Vojnic, Plaski, and Korenica units, as well as the JNA and police units from these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Same question: Milos Pajic; what would you expect him to have said and why would you have expected him to say if there was more than one unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it would have been an obligation on his part to make aware us, representatives of the civilian authorities, of the appearance of a unit in the territory where we were politically active. For instance, I was active in the territory of the -- of Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Same question in relation to commanders of the TO staffs; what kind of discussions were you having with them where you might have expected there to have been mention of more than one unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Milan Babic had appointed them to these posts. We had meetings of the civilian authorities, TO, and the police discussing the general situation in Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And finally: Which meetings involved the representatives of the JNA wherein you might have expected to hear about more than one unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October of 1991 I became a member of the zone staff charged with providing information. I became director of radio and television Petrova Gora. Where military and other issues were discussed, I would attend these meetings, as well as others, Mr. Paspalj and Cedo Bulat who was the head of the military training-grounds Slunj. And the elements of the command structure of the 5th Military District was there. So Cedo Bulat and other officers, Mirko Radak, would also attend these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what did the meetings involve? What was the purpose of them?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To see how the TO could help man JNA units, to see what their strength was, what the general situation was in the area covered by the zone staff, what the situation was like for the population, and the developments in the area in general. The zone staff also covered Banija at the time; in other words, it was the zone staff for Kordun and Banija.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time. I've only got about 10 minutes, if Your Honour would allow that, after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- of course, primarily, we take the 75 minutes instead of the usually 90 because of Mr. Stanisic. If Mr. Stanisic would enable you to have the next ten minutes, then of course it's fine as far as the Chamber is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To be honest, I would rather have a break just so that I can gather the material and be efficient after the break if that's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- yes, that's -- I'm not going to say it's fine, but it's accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I want to just very briefly discuss a period around the time of the Vance Plan negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could we have on the screen 65 ter 1385.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What is going to come up on the screen are minutes or a stenographic record of the 188th Session of the Presidency of the Socialist Federative -- Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, held on the 25th of February, 1992. And you can see there who attended the session. And you can see there the participants included Petar Gracanin, federal secretary of the interior. Now, did you attend this session or were you privy to the preparations for the session or the subjects that were discussed during the session?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has to do with Vance Plan. You said Vance-Owen Plan, whereas it's the Vance Plan. I didn't attend this Presidency session. But in the capacity of the Presidency of the Assembly of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, I attended several meetings of the Presidency where the Vance Plan was discussed. This is already at the stage where the Vance Plan is being accepted, in preparation of the Assembly session which was to take place, I believe, in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Mr. Babic's position was that he opposed the Vance Plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you agree with that position?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, and I suppose that was the reason why I was chosen to be part of the delegation of the RSK, one of the seven delegates taking part in the negotiations in the Presidency of Yugoslavia in late 1991 and early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to page 8 of the English and 8 of the B/C/S. And we can see there that Petar Gracanin is speaking. Now, just now we've oriented ourselves with who is speaking. Let's move on to page 11 of the English and 11 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And halfway down the English page Petar Gracanin notes: "As for the Internal Affairs organs in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, we need to find a proper balance there, from the request from these 34.000 people, and what we did on Saturday and Sunday together with their organs, but these are organs that were consulted more from the legal aspect, and a balance should probably be found there. We gave around 4.000 for the entire --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "We gave around 4.000" ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "We gave around 4.000 for the entire area, but that is just the core. We should look to find a middle way where the police force is needed." So we have the Federal Secretary of the Interior talking about giving 4.000 people for the entire area of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. "We should look to find a middle way where the police force is needed." Are you able to cast any light on what the federal secretary of interior is talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the provisions of the Vance Plan, which reads that in the area of the RSK or, rather, in the UN-protected area, the only presence allowed is that of the police force, and now discussions are taking place about the strength of the police force that should remain in the area after the arrival of the United Nations peace forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Gracanin is talking about the Federal Ministry of Interior -- or the federal Secretary of the Interior giving 4.000. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not the federal secretariat providing the men. They are charged with co-ordinating this issue with the bodies of the RSK, because the RSK had asked for 34.000 men hailing from our area to be trained as policemen. The co-ordinator was Petar Gracanin because the negotiations around the Vance Plan were conducted on the level of Yugoslavia. In other words, it was Yugoslavia negotiating with the United Nations the implementation of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who gave 4.000 men?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were supposed to provide them, at their proposal. In other words, these were supposed to be individuals present in the RSK. However, the original agreement -- or, rather, the agreement was only in respect of 4.000 men, rather than 34.000 that we had requested, and I suppose this was the result of the negotiations conducted between Petar Gracanin and the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did any of this involve the Republic of Serbia MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The negotiations and meetings I attended did not include representatives of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. There were representatives of the federal organs, General Staff, representatives of what was at that time -- well, the Serbian part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to page 27 of the B/C/S and 28 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And to orientate yourself, the speaker here is Andjelko Maslic, who was the general secretary of the Presidency of the SFRY. And he notes, at page 28 of the English: "They think that they will stay the day after tomorrow to hold a session of the government and to adopt specific conclusions, obligations that concern the arrival of the peace forces. There is a proposal that Martic should explain the organisational plan of the Internal Affairs in Krajina. A team working on producing the Law on Internal Affairs or, rather, joining the laws that already exist in these parts, together with certain amendments where they differ, adopt a single law. This has been proposed for other laws too." Are you able to cast any light on that remark?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the refusal on the part of Milan Babic and some of the deputies of the SDS to accept the Vance Plan, without his approval the Assembly meeting in Glina accepted the Vance Plan. These were preparations for a large Assembly session which was held in Borovo Selo, where a new leadership of the RSK was elected. Goran Hadzic was elected president, Mila Paspalj re-elected speaker of the Assembly, and I think Mr. Zecevic was prime minister. At that Assembly session there was no one from among Babic's followers, if I can call him that, and I wasn't there either, where there was the -- where there was a representation from Yugoslavia as well, as we can see from these discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stanisic, as far as you were aware, take part in any of these meetings and negotiations and discussions?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. And for the two or three Presidency sessions that I attended, once there was Mr. Milosevic on behalf of Serbia, once there was Mr. Bozovic, I think he was the prime minister of Serbia, but also included were representatives of Montenegro, Mr. Bulatovic and Momir Bulatovic, Biljana Plavsic, Radovan Karadzic from Bosnia, at that last session when we were under pressure from them to accept the Vance Plan and we refused. In other words, the meetings that I attended did not include Mr. Stanisic. I'm sorry if I expanded in answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And finally, in relation to this Presidency session, you can see at page 27 of the B/C/S and 27 of -- sorry, 28 of the English, the continuation of that speech wherein it says: "Just before going to the session, comrades from the federal SUP informed me that when Martic comes today, they will try to co-ordinate this again, but that there is an inclination to increase this number, possibly by one battalion. I do not think that it should go beyond 10.000 or 12.000." Can you cast any light on this and the discussions between the federal SUP and Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't attend these discussions, so I wouldn't know about it. It was only natural for Martic to be present there, in view of the fact that a new government had not been elected yet. And the federal government and its organs were a guarantor for our side in the Vance Plan. That's why they co-ordinated their activities with Martic, because the 4.000 men we asked for were supposed to constitute the local police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this as an exhibit, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be D318, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D318 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So this is the final questions, Mr. Bosnic. You mentioned you first met Mr. Stanisic in 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever meet him after that point?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not until I was called to testify to the events happening in the Krajina and Croatia for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you speak to him during 1994 and afterwards until the point where you were called to testify? Did you have any personal contact whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you spoke yesterday about speaking to Babic before he came to The Hague, and are you able to just shed a little light on what you perceived of his mental state at that point?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I don't know that the witness is a psychologist or can comment on someone's mental state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness has said he was one of his closest friends. He can indicate whether he felt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He can make factual observations in relation to what he considers may be in relation with the mental state of Mr. Babic. And he should limit himself to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you follow that, Mr. Bosnic? Could you limit yourself to what you observed about Mr. Babic's mental state before he left to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The madam was right in saying that I am not a psychologist, but we did know each other for a long time. What I experienced was first great disappointment and then rage because nobody in Serbia would respond to his requests to advise him on his subsequent steps and to help him with his family. He was disappointed and angry. That's how I would characterise him, in layman's terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you never saw him again before his sad and unfortunate suicide; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the last time I saw him was when he said that he would drag into the mud everyone else along with himself. I saw him in person on that occasion for the last time, and then I saw him while he was in The Hague and I was shocked by his statements and demeanour. How shocked I was you could tell from the opening remarks I made where I said, as the saying goes in our people, that it is better for a man to lose his life than his honour and honesty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I think we asked for factual observations in relation to the mental state of Mr. Babic. What we get in an answer to that is the apparent -- what this witness thinks about Mr. Babic's behaviour. And I don't think that that's what we were asking him for, because he is implicitly saying that Mr. Babic was not a man honour, that's at least how I understand that, and that's not something that I would expect as an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that's Your Honour's view, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So finally, Mr. Bosnic, having not known Mr. Stanisic but known Mr. Babic very well, why did you decide to give evidence for the Stanisic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Mr. Babic was not telling the truth, even though he was a friend of mine and I still regard him as one. The Milan Babic I knew between 1991 and 1995 and 1996 is not the same Babic who appeared before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've got nothing further. Thank you, Mr. Bosnic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Petrovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bosnic.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I should like to follow up with a couple of questions, the topic that you just discussed with my colleague, Mr. Jordash. Did you know Mr. Babic's wife?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know her.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Babic's wife addressed the public after the demise of her husband? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After coming to Belgrade she talked to the public, after actually returning to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the content of her public address?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read something about it. It was published in the "Politika," but I cannot recall the exact text.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go through the questions which were raised awhile ago while it is still fresh in our memories. We looked at these minutes of the session of the SFRY Presidency and a question was raised regarding the 4.000 policemen mentioned by Petar Gracanin. My question to you is: Do you know that the federal Secretariat of the Interior with Petar Gracanin at the helm at the time was only proposing the structure of the MUP of the Republic of Serbian Krajina; it actually only proposed how under the circumstances that the ministry should look?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, how it should look and what strength it should have when the United Nations representatives came, because according to Vance Plan only the police could carry arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And the personnel and the command structure of the ministry would remain as envisaged under the the laws of the Serbian Krajina at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, that is correct. I cannot say in respect of every individual, but to the best of my knowledge all the chiefs of the SUPs, all the komandirs, all the chiefs remained working as policemen but only had a larger complement of people assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Bosnic, let us pause between question and answer because we speak the same language and it is difficult for the interpreters to keep abreast of us. Tell me, let us briefly touch upon the question of the Vance Plan. Perhaps it was not quite clear to me what capacity you participated in the negotiations regarding the Vance Plan Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly actually elected 7 MPs who represented the Assembly of the Serbian Krajina in these negotiations in the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you were one these seven elected representatives?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The seven-member delegation that we are talking about negotiated with whom; who was the second or the third negotiating side in the process?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These meetings in the Presidency were actually pressure exerted on the leadership of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina to accept the Vance Plan. In addition to ourselves, to us seven, there were four members of the Presidency: Yugoslav Kostic, Branko Kostic, Sejdo Bajramovic, and a fourth one whose name I cannot recall at this point. So representatives of the federal government, the minister of the interior, the federal one, Petar Gracanin, the Chief of General Staff Blagoje Adzic, representatives of Montenegro, Milo Djukanovic, Momir Bulatovic, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bosnic, were you familiar with the draft of that agreement which was to be signed on behalf of both the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time? Do you know what the basic content of the agreement was?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: What was in the proposed draft agreement that posed the greatest problem to you from the Republic of the Serbian Krajina for you to accept the offered text of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the basic thing was that in the preamble of the Vance Plan it was written that it was Croatian territory under the protection of the United Nations, whereas we thought that they were coming to conditionally return us to the Republic of Croatia. Secondly, we asked in the military section to apply the system of dividing the warring parties and not an ink-blot system. And thirdly, we were not sure how much -- we were not certain how secure we would be if the JNA left the territory, and we wanted the Serbian areas which did not belong to the Serbian municipalities in the area of the Republic of Serbian Krajina to be also covered by the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood your answer now, these are the sticking points between you and what the positions of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, was this agreement finally accepted and how was it accepted?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, eventually it was accepted with opposition on the part of Milan Babic, myself, and some other people. It was accepted on behalf of the Assembly of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina by the president of the Assembly and a member of our delegation, Mile Paspalj, who, like ourselves, up to the last minute of that meeting which lasted about 50 minutes was opposed to the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of -- on what basis did Mile Paspalj accept that agreement on behalf of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was actually a trick. Although Milan Babic was in Belgrade, he was not in the Presidency then. The explanation was that Milan Babic could not attend the session and being absent and he was deputised for by the speaker, by the president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a second. In listing the present members of the SFRY Presidency, Borislav Jovic was not mentioned. Did he participate in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did participate. And sometimes he chaired the sessions and sometimes it was Branko Kostic, the representative of Montenegro, who presided over these sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the signing of this agreement in the way that you have described, did the peace forces of the United Nations deploy -- start to deploy in the field in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, i.e., the Republic of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because we could do nothing through our organs of authority, in agreement with Serbia we opted to accept the United Nations forces. But according to the Vance Plan, they communicated with, as they put it, the local authorities and the local leaders, including myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: By the signing of this agreement and the deployment of their forces, did the UN -- of the UN, after that did the war stop in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that stage, yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What were the relations like between Milan Babic and the representatives of the SFRY, later the FRY, after the events that we are talking about, namely the signing and acceptance of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relations cooled and Milan Babic practically remained without any levers of power, but he managed to remain the mayor of Knin municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Milan Babic try to form some sort of a new military organisation after the signing of the Vance agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, unless you mean the "Garda King Peter," King Peter's Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I should ask you specifically. First let me ask you this, although you have already said so: So the Vance Plan prohibited the existence of military units in the territory of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that in April 1992 Babic gathered some members of the territory in the defence of the MUP of the Krajina and tried to establish the so-called Serbian army? This was in the village of Kosevo, not far from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate in that, but I had heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the witness be shown Exhibit P1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, please take a look at the first paragraph of this document of the Prosecutor and tell me whether what is in the first paragraph is consistent with your memory of the events that we have just discussed. Just the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the people who are referred to here. They are from the SDS leadership, so that they probably attended this gathering, but I myself did not, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please just tell us, if you know, who Mirko Jovic is, who is mentioned as one of the people attending this gathering.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Jovic was the president of one right-wing party in Serbia, and I believe that he had some sort of a paramilitary unit. Whether they were some White Eagles or something like that, I'm not quite certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the political options of Mirko Jovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing in particular, except that he was of the right-wing hue and that he did not represent any relevant force in Serbia and that he had this unit. This paramilitary unit which I believe participated in fighting in Western Slavonia and Bosnia, but don't take my word for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I hear that you're encouraging the witness to make a pause. I encourage you to do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I should do my best. Can we have page 3 shown to the witness in the B/C/S. I believe that it is also the third page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, please take a look at the first paragraph on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for Your Honours, I believe that we shall -- I hope that we shall soon have the English-language version on the screen. Yes, it is the second paragraph in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, have you taken a look at it?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question to you is this: Did the Vance Plan foresee that all weapons of the former Army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina would be stored and would be kept under key, practically that the army would be disarmed?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to the double-key system. The keys to the storehouse would be held by a representative of the United Nations and a representative of the Territorial Defence after the disarming.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The call, which we can see in this paragraph, to the effect that weapons should not be returned, which was actually made by Mirko Jovic, is a call to violate the Vance agreement which had been accepted a couple of months before that?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This attempt at creating a Serbian army, had it been successful, would have been a violation of the provisions of the Vance agreement; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would. It would have been that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, yesterday you referred to the fact that the policy of the SDS was to actually pre-empt every step of the Croatian status by an adequate move on the part of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the general concept in principle how we functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And if I understood you correctly, that meant that if Croatia organized a referendum, the Serbian Krajina would organise a referendum also. And, in fact, before, if Croatia was to amend its constitution, the Serbs would also adopt their constitution.
